title: Flexible Kernels for Protein Property Prediction
claim: Raw substitution scores give near-diagonal correlation that treats most residues as unrelated; a power transform reveals graded similarity structure.
layout: 2 side-by-side heatmaps with shared colorbar, annotated cell values, left-to-right comparison
description: Two 4x4 blue heatmaps of correlations among the amino acids V, I, W and C, with a shared colorbar from 0 to 1 on the far right. The left matrix is the BLOSUM50 substitution matrix as a correlation matrix. It is almost entirely pale, except for a dark diagonal of 1.00 values and a mid-blue V–I cell at 0.37. Every other off-diagonal entry is tiny and printed in scientific notation, such as 2×10^-6 and 6×10^-9. The right matrix is the same matrix raised to the power 0.03. Its off-diagonal values are now graded and moderate: V–I is 0.97, V–W is 0.68, C–W is 0.57, and the others fall between 0.68 and 0.75. Each cell shows its number in bold white text with a dark outline. The eye goes first to the dark diagonal and the contrast between the pale left panel and the saturated right panel.
caption: The BLOSUM50 substitution matrix as a correlation matrix. We zoom-in on four amino acids, two of which are biophysically similar (valine and isoleucine) and two of which are largely dissimilar to all other amino acids (tryptophan and cysteine). The matrix on the right has been raised to the power 0.03. For details on the normalization scheme we use refer to Sec. A.3. For the full matrix see Fig. 16.
abstract: Despite its importance to applications in protein design, predicting protein properties like binding affinity and thermostability from sparse experimental data remains a significant challenge. Accordingly, we introduce a class of sequence kernels that exploit evolutionary substitution matrices as well as local linearity and demonstrate that the resulting Gaussian processes provide data-efficient models of protein property landscapes, frequently outperforming alternatives that rely on foundation model embeddings. Furthermore--by learning what are in effect structure-aware substitution matrices--we show that our kernels can readily incorporate structural information from foundation models. We demonstrate that these structure-conditioned kernels are well suited to multi-task learning across multiple protein property landscapes and can decisively outperform local supervised learning methods.
